title: Defining scope: outputs, outcomes, benefits & PBS/WBS/CBS
blurb: Define scope as outputs, outcomes and benefits, then break it down with a PBS, WBS and CBS that leave nothing out.
question: A leisure centre group is building an online booking system. The sponsor asks the project manager to 'define the scope properly' so nothing is missed and everyone agrees what success looks like. How should the scope be described, and which breakdown structures would the project manager use?

teach.h: Scope is more than a list of deliverables
teach.body: Scope is the totality of the outputs, outcomes and benefits, and the work needed to produce them. In plain English: what the project will hand over, what will change when people use it, the measurable gain that change brings, and all the work to get there. Defining scope in all three terms ties the project to its business case, so the team builds the right thing and stakeholders agree what is in, and what is out.

steps.label: Output
steps.sub: Online booking app and website, staff trained

steps.label: Outcome
steps.sub: Members book classes online instead of phoning

steps.label: Benefit
steps.sub: Reception calls fall and class fill rates rise, measured monthly

teach.caption: The project delivers the output. The outcome and benefit happen when the business uses it, which is why benefits are often realised after handover.
A benefit must be measurable. 'Happier members' is vague; 'complaints down by a quarter' can be tracked.

teach.body: A project that defines only outputs can deliver everything on the list and still fail, because nothing proved those outputs would create the benefits. Clear scope gives the business case something to trace to, sets the basis for estimates, plans and success criteria, and draws the boundary: what is included and, just as important, what is explicitly excluded. Unwritten exclusions are where disputes, rework and scope creep begin.

teach.caption: The PBS breaks the scope into products (nouns): WHAT will be delivered. Include the 'soft' products such as training and communications, or they get missed.
The WBS is derived from the PBS: the work needed to produce each product. Its lowest level is the work package, small enough to estimate, schedule and give to one owner.

head: Work package
Labour
Other costs
Total
teach.caption: The CBS maps costs to the WBS work packages. Overspends can then be traced to the exact part of the work, not just seen as a project total.

teach.text: Classic confusion: the PBS lists PRODUCTS (what), the WBS lists the WORK to make them, and the CBS lists their COSTS. Order: PBS, then WBS, then CBS. A task list is not a WBS, and a WBS organised by department rather than by deliverable leaves gaps and duplication. Also don't call a benefit an outcome: the outcome is the change, the benefit is its measurable value.

teach.h: Defining scope in linear vs iterative life cycles

rows.label: When detailed
values: High level first, detail per time box

rows.label: What flexes
values: Time and cost, via change control

teach.caption: Both still define outputs, outcomes and benefits. Iterative projects fix the benefits they are aiming for, then let the detailed outputs evolve.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define scope as outputs (deliverables), outcomes (the change) and benefits (measurable improvement), with an example of each.
Explain that the PBS identifies every product, so the scope is complete and nothing is missed.
Explain that the WBS breaks those products into work packages that can be estimated, scheduled and owned.
Explain that the CBS maps costs to the work packages, giving budget control and traceable variances.
Add the boundary: state inclusions and exclusions, then baseline and control the scope.
Scope = outputs, outcomes and benefits, plus the work to produce them.
Output: what's handed over. Outcome: the change. Benefit: the measurable gain.
PBS (products) comes first; the WBS (work packages) is derived from it; the CBS maps costs to the WBS.
State exclusions explicitly to prevent disputes and scope creep.
Linear: full breakdown baselined early. Iterative: high level first, refined each time box.

summary: You can now define scope in terms of outputs, outcomes and benefits and tell the three apart in a scenario. You can also explain how a PBS, a WBS derived from it and a CBS mapped to it make the scope complete, plannable and controllable in both linear and iterative projects.

A.q: A council project replaces old street lights with LED lanterns. Which of the following is an OUTCOME of the project?
options: New LED lanterns fitted to 4,000 lamp posts
Street-lighting energy bills fall by 30%
More residents now choose to walk at night
A lantern maintenance manual for the depot
A.why: An outcome is the changed circumstance or behaviour that results when the outputs are used: residents walking at night because the streets are better lit.

whyNot.0: The fitted lanterns are the project's output: the deliverable it hands over.
whyNot.1: A measurable 30% fall in energy bills is a benefit: the quantified improvement.
whyNot.3: The maintenance manual is another output (a product handed over to operations).

A.q: Which statement best describes the difference between a product breakdown structure (PBS) and a work breakdown structure (WBS)?
options: PBS shows what's delivered; WBS the work for it
PBS shows who does the work; WBS what each costs
PBS is for linear projects; WBS is for iterative
PBS lists the activities; WBS lists the products
A.why: The PBS breaks the scope into the products to be delivered (what). The WBS breaks down the work needed to produce those products into work packages.

whyNot.1: Who does the work is shown by the OBS and responsibility matrix; costs are shown by the CBS.
whyNot.2: Both structures can be used in either life cycle; they are not tied to one model.
whyNot.3: This reverses them: the PBS holds products and the WBS holds the work.

A.q: In what order are the three breakdown structures normally developed?
options: WBS, then PBS, then CBS
CBS, then WBS, then PBS
PBS, then CBS, then WBS
PBS, then WBS, then CBS
A.why: First identify every product (PBS), then the work needed to make each one (WBS), then map costs to those work packages (CBS).

whyNot.0: The WBS is derived from the products, so the PBS must come first.
whyNot.1: You cannot cost work you have not yet broken down, so the CBS comes last.
whyNot.2: The CBS is mapped to the WBS work packages, so it can't come before the WBS.

B.q: Halfway through a school IT refresh, teachers ask why the project is not replacing the classroom whiteboards. Nobody can find anything in writing either way. What would most likely have prevented this?
options: Adding more detail to the activity list
Building the CBS before drawing the WBS
Stating the scope's exclusions explicitly
Holding a lessons-learned review at close
B.why: Scope boundaries need inclusions AND exclusions stated explicitly and agreed. Unwritten exclusions lead to assumptions, disputes and scope creep.

whyNot.0: More activity detail doesn't say what is out of scope; the gap is the missing boundary.
whyNot.1: The CBS comes after the WBS and is about cost, not the scope boundary.
whyNot.3: A closure review is too late to prevent a dispute that arises mid-project.

B.q: Which statement best describes a work package?
options: A top-level product at the head of the PBS
A pot of money held back as contingency
A lowest-level WBS element with one owner
A list of the stakeholders the work affects
B.why: A work package is the lowest level of the WBS: a defined piece of work small enough to estimate, schedule, cost and assign to a single owner.

whyNot.0: The top of the PBS is the final product, not a work package.
whyNot.1: Contingency is a budget reserve for risk, not a unit of work.
whyNot.3: A list of affected people is a stakeholder list, not part of the WBS.

B.q: Why should a project's scope be defined in terms of benefits as well as outputs?
options: Outputs can be delivered yet still add no value
Benefits are easier to cost than the outputs
Benefits remove the need for acceptance criteria
Outputs only exist in iterative life cycles
B.why: Defining benefits links the scope to the business case. Without them, a project can hand over every output and still fail to deliver the improvement it was funded for.

whyNot.1: Benefits are usually harder to measure and cost than outputs, not easier.
whyNot.2: Outputs still need acceptance criteria to show they are fit for purpose.
whyNot.3: Every project, linear or iterative, produces outputs.

C.q: A project manager lists the work for a hospital car park under each department involved (estates, IT, finance). Stakeholders cannot confirm that every output is covered. What is the best corrective step?
options: Add a separate cost breakdown per department
Replace the WBS with a detailed Gantt chart
Ask each department to re-estimate its tasks
Build a PBS first and derive the WBS from it
C.why: A WBS organised by department rather than by deliverable leaves gaps and duplication. Identifying every product in a PBS first, then deriving the work from it, makes scope coverage complete and checkable.

whyNot.0: Costing by department keeps the same structural flaw and says nothing about missing outputs.
whyNot.1: A Gantt chart schedules the work; it doesn't prove that all deliverables are covered.
whyNot.2: Better estimates of the same task list still won't reveal missing products.

C.q: A digital team delivers a new customer portal in two-week time boxes. How will its scope breakdown most likely be handled?
options: Full WBS baselined in Definition, then frozen
High-level product set, detailed per time box
No breakdown, since the backlog replaces scope
A CBS only, because time and cost are fixed
C.why: In an iterative life cycle the scope is defined at a high level first (the product set and backlog), then broken down in detail time box by time box as requirements emerge.

whyNot.0: A full, frozen WBS set in Definition is the linear approach, and Definition is a linear phase.
whyNot.2: The backlog is a way of holding and prioritising scope; the scope is still defined and broken down.
whyNot.3: Fixed time and cost don't remove the need to define what will be delivered.

C.q: A museum is building a new visitor centre. Which THREE belong in its scope definition? 1: the exhibition fit-out. 2: visitors staying longer on site. 3: a 15% rise in café income. 4: the contractor's daily timesheets.
options: 1, 2 and 4
1, 2 and 3
1, 3 and 4
2, 3 and 4
C.why: Scope covers outputs (the fit-out), outcomes (visitors staying longer) and benefits (a measurable rise in café income). Timesheets are a record of effort, not part of the scope.

whyNot.0: Timesheets (4) are a progress and cost record, not an output, outcome or benefit; it misses the benefit (3).
whyNot.2: This drops the outcome (2) and wrongly includes timesheets (4).
whyNot.3: This drops the output (1), the thing the project actually delivers, and includes timesheets (4).

reteach.title: Think of a kitchen refit
reteach.question: A family is having a new kitchen fitted. What would its outputs, outcomes and benefits be, and how would a fitter break the job down?

blocks.body: The outputs are the things the fitter hands over: units, worktops, appliances, new lighting. The outcome is what changes when the family uses them: they cook at home and eat together instead of buying takeaways. The benefit is the measurable gain: perhaps £150 a month saved on takeaways. The fitter's job list only covers the outputs, which is why the family must agree the outcomes and benefits they want before choosing the design.

blocks.h: The kitchen PBS, then the work
blocks.caption: Each product (PBS) gets the work needed to make it (WBS), and each piece of work gets a price (CBS).

blocks.text: If the quote says nothing about tiling, expect an argument later. Write down what is excluded, not just what is included.

explain.body: Outputs are the deliverables the project produces. Outcomes are the changed circumstances or behaviours when people use them. Benefits are the measurable improvements that result, which justify the investment. Scope covers all three, plus the work to produce the outputs.

test.q: Which is the best description of an outcome?
options: The tangible product handed over at the end
The changed situation when outputs are used
The measurable gain the sponsor reports on
The work done by the team in a work package
test.why: An outcome is the changed circumstance or behaviour that results from using the outputs.

whyNot.0: A tangible product handed over is an output.
whyNot.2: A measurable gain is a benefit, which flows from the outcome.
whyNot.3: Work in a work package produces outputs; it is not an outcome.

explain.body: A PBS is a hierarchy of everything the project must produce, from the final product down to its components. It answers WHAT will be delivered, and it is the best check that the scope is complete, including documents, training and other 'soft' products.

test.q: A PBS is drawn mainly to answer which question?
options: Who will carry out each task?
How much will each item cost?
In what order is the work done?
What will the project produce?
test.why: The PBS identifies all the products (deliverables) the project must produce.

whyNot.0: Who does what is shown by the OBS and responsibility assignment matrix.
whyNot.1: Costs are shown in the CBS.
whyNot.2: Sequence is shown in the schedule (network diagram or Gantt chart).

explain.body: The WBS breaks down the work needed to produce each product, usually derived from the PBS. Its lowest level is the work package. Because every work package links to a product, nothing is missed and nothing extra creeps in. The WBS is the basis for estimating, scheduling, costing and assigning work.

test.q: A WBS review finds several tasks that cannot be linked to any product in the PBS. What does this most likely show?
options: The PBS was drawn too early in the project
Work has crept in beyond the agreed scope
The tasks are on the critical path instead
The CBS has not yet been mapped to the WBS
test.why: Every work package should trace to a product. Work with no product behind it is outside the agreed scope: a sign of scope creep or gold-plating.

whyNot.0: Drawing the PBS first is correct practice, not the cause.
whyNot.2: Being on the critical path is about timing; it doesn't explain why tasks have no product.
whyNot.3: The CBS follows the WBS; its absence doesn't create untraceable tasks.

explain.body: The CBS breaks the project budget down by mapping costs (labour, materials, equipment and so on) to the WBS work packages. That lets the project manager build the budget from the bottom up and see exactly where any variance comes from.

test.q: A finance director can't see which part of a project is overspending, because costs are only recorded as a project total. What would help most?
options: A CBS mapped to the WBS work packages
A larger contingency reserve for risk
A PBS that lists the main deliverables
A monthly highlight report to the board
test.why: Mapping costs to work packages through a CBS shows budget against actual for each part of the work, so variances can be traced and explained.

whyNot.1: More contingency hides the problem rather than locating it.
whyNot.2: A PBS lists products, not costs.
whyNot.3: A report built on a project-level total still can't show where the overspend is.
